sessions.title: HTML Basics: Document Structure
sessions.content:
Every web page begins with a doctype declaration that tells the browser which version of HTML to render. The root element encloses the entire document, and it is divided into two primary sections: and . The contains metadata such as , character encoding, and links to external resources like CSS files. The <body> holds the visible content, including headings, paragraphs, images, and links. Understanding the hierarchy—doctype → html → head/body → content—is crucial because browsers rely on this structure to correctly interpret and display the page. Below is a minimal yet complete HTML5 document: ```html <!DOCTYPE html> <html lang="en"> <head> <meta charset="UTF-8"> <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"> <title>My First Page

Welcome to My Site

This paragraph demonstrates basic text content.

``` Notice the indentation and closing tags; they improve readability and prevent parsing errors. Even though browsers can tolerate some missing tags, writing well‑formed HTML ensures consistent behavior across all user agents and aids accessibility tools.

sessions.title: CSS Fundamentals: Selectors and Box Model
sessions.content:
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) applies visual styles to HTML elements. Selectors define which elements receive a rule; they can be type selectors (e.g., p), class selectors (e.g., .highlight), ID selectors (e.g., #main), or attribute selectors (e.g., [type="text"]). The cascade resolves conflicts by specificity and source order. Every element is rendered as a rectangular box consisting of content, padding, border, and margin. The content area holds the actual text or media; padding adds space inside the border; the border surrounds the padding; margin creates space outside the border, separating the element from its neighbors. Modifying any of these properties changes layout. Below is an example that styles a paragraph with a class "note" and demonstrates the box model: ```html

This paragraph demonstrates the CSS box model.

``` If you inspect the element in a browser's developer tools, you will see the total rendered width equals content width + left/right padding + left/right border + left/right margin. Mastering selectors and the box model is essential for any layout work.

sessions.objective: Understand how CSS selectors target elements and how the box model determines element dimensions and spacing.

sessions.title: Variables and Data Types
choices: A const variable cannot be reassigned, and the value it references is always immutable.
A const variable can be redeclared within the same block scope.
A const variable cannot be reassigned, but if it holds an object, the object's properties can still be changed.
A const variable behaves exactly like a var variable but with block scope.
sessions.content: JavaScript provides three ways to declare variables: var, let, and const. The var keyword is function‑scoped and can be redeclared, which often leads to unexpected bugs due to hoisting. let introduces block‑scoping, preventing accidental redeclaration within the same block, and is the preferred choice for mutable values. const also uses block‑scoping but creates a read‑only binding; the variable identifier cannot be reassigned, though the value it points to may still be mutable if it is an object or array. JavaScript's primitive types include Number, String, Boolean, Null, Undefined, Symbol, and BigInt. Numbers are double‑precision floating‑point values; strings are immutable sequences of UTF‑16 code units; booleans represent true/false; null is an intentional absence of any object value; undefined indicates a variable that has been declared but not assigned a value; Symbol creates unique identifiers; and BigInt enables representation of integers beyond the safe 2^53‑1 limit. Understanding these basics is crucial for writing predictable code and for later TypeScript type annotations.
sessions.exercise: Write a snippet that declares a mutable counter using let, a constant PI using const, and demonstrates the difference between undefined and null by logging their types and values.
sessions.question: Which statement about const is correct?
sessions.objective: Learn the differences between var, let, const and the primary primitive data types in JavaScript.

sessions.title: Asynchronous Programming with Promises
choices: It receives the resolved value and can transform it before the next then.
It executes a callback only if the Promise was fulfilled successfully.
It runs a callback after the Promise settles, regardless of fulfillment or rejection.
It replaces the need for both then and catch handlers.
sessions.content: Asynchronous operations in JavaScript are often handled with Promises, which represent a value that may be available now, later, or never. A Promise is created with the constructor new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... }). Inside the executor function, you call resolve(value) when the operation succeeds, or reject(error) when it fails. Consumers attach handlers using then(onFulfilled) for successful resolution and catch(onRejected) for errors. Promise chaining allows sequential asynchronous steps: each then returns a new Promise, enabling the next then to receive the transformed result. The finally method runs a callback regardless of outcome, useful for cleanup. Importantly, unhandled rejections propagate up the chain, so always provide a catch or finally to avoid silent failures. Understanding the event loop, microtasks, and how Promises fit into it helps avoid race conditions and ensures predictable execution order.
sessions.exercise: Create a Promise that resolves after 2 seconds with the message "Done". Chain a then to log the message, and add a catch to handle any potential errors.
sessions.question: What does the finally method do in a Promise chain?
sessions.objective: Understand how to create, chain, and handle errors with JavaScript Promises.

sessions.title: Basic Types and Interfaces
sessions.content: TypeScript extends JavaScript by adding static type annotations that are checked at compile time. Primitive types include number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, and bigint, mirroring JavaScript's runtime types. You can annotate variables, function parameters, and return types to catch mismatches early. Interfaces provide a way to describe the shape of an object, specifying required properties, optional properties (using ?), and readonly modifiers. For example, interface Person { name: string; age?: number; readonly id: string; } describes an object that must have a name and id, while age is optional. TypeScript also supports union types (e.g., string | number) and literal types (e.g., 'admin' | 'user'), enabling precise modeling of data structures. Using these features helps prevent common bugs, such as passing the wrong type to a function or accessing undefined properties.
sessions.exercise: Define an interface called "Product" with properties: id (string, readonly), name (string), price (number), and an optional description (string). Then create a variable of type Product and assign appropriate values.
sessions.question: Which of the following correctly declares a variable that can hold either a string or a number?
sessions.objective: Introduce TypeScript's type annotations, primitive types, and how interfaces describe object shapes.

sessions.title: Generics and Advanced Types
choices: T must be a string literal type.
T must be a type that can be used as an object key, i.e., string, number, or symbol.
T must be an object with a numeric index signature.
T must be a union of all possible primitive types.
sessions.content: Generics enable you to write reusable components that work with a variety of types while preserving type information. A generic type parameter is declared inside angle brackets, e.g., function identity<T>(arg: T): T { return arg; }. This function can accept any type, and the compiler infers the specific type on each call. Constraints restrict the set of types a generic can accept, using the extends keyword. For instance, function getLength<T extends { length: number }>(obj: T): number { return obj.length; } ensures that the argument has a length property. TypeScript also provides utility types like Partial<T>, Readonly<T>, and Pick<T, K>. Advanced techniques such as conditional types (e.g., T extends U ? X : Y) allow you to express type transformations based on relationships. Mastering generics leads to type‑safe libraries and APIs that adapt to many data shapes without sacrificing compile‑time safety.
sessions.exercise: Write a generic function called "wrapInArray" that takes a value of any type and returns an array containing that value. Use a type parameter to preserve the input type.
sessions.question: What does the constraint "T extends keyof any" guarantee about the generic type T?
sessions.objective: Learn how to write generic functions and use constraints to enforce type relationships.

sessions.title: Understanding Tables and Data Types
sessions.content:
PostgreSQL stores data in relational tables where each column has a defined data type. Common types include INTEGER for whole numbers, VARCHAR(n) for variable‑length strings, TEXT for unlimited text, DATE for calendar dates, and BOOLEAN for true/false values. When creating a table, you declare each column with its type and optionally add constraints such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, or PRIMARY KEY. The PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each row and automatically creates a unique index, which speeds up look‑ups. Choosing the right data type improves storage efficiency and query performance. For example, using SMALLINT instead of INTEGER for a column that only stores values 0‑255 reduces disk space. Additionally, PostgreSQL supports domain types and ENUMs for more expressive schemas. Understanding these fundamentals enables you to design robust schemas that scale and maintain data integrity.

Example:
```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    last_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    hire_date DATE NOT NULL,
    salary NUMERIC(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0),
    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE
);
```
sessions.exercise: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a `products` table with columns: `product_id` (auto‑increment primary key), `name` (VARCHAR up to 100, not null), `price` (NUMERIC with two decimal places, must be positive), `in_stock` (BOOLEAN default true), and `created_at` (TIMESTAMP with default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP).
sessions.question: Which constraint automatically creates a unique index in PostgreSQL?
sessions.objective: Learn how to define tables, choose appropriate data types, and enforce primary keys in PostgreSQL.

sessions.title: Advanced Queries: Joins and Indexes
choices: Only rows that have matches in both tables
Rows from the left table with NULLs for right‑hand columns
Rows from the right table with NULLs for left‑hand columns
sessions.content:
Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on related columns. An INNER JOIN returns rows with matching values in both tables, while LEFT (or RIGHT) OUTER JOIN returns all rows from one table and matching rows from the other, filling non‑matching columns with NULL. Proper indexing is crucial: an index on the join column allows PostgreSQL to locate matching rows quickly, reducing the need for full table scans. Composite indexes can cover multiple columns, and partial indexes can target rows that meet a condition, further optimizing performance. EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals the query plan and shows whether indexes are used. Understanding when to create indexes—especially on foreign key columns used in joins—helps maintain responsive applications as data volume grows.

Example:
```sql
-- Create indexes on foreign key columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id);

-- Perform a join using the indexed column
SELECT o.order_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';
```

Also, create an index that would help this query.
sessions.question: What does a LEFT OUTER JOIN return when there is no matching row in the right‑hand table?
sessions.objective: Master inner and outer joins, and learn how indexes improve query performance in PostgreSQL.

sessions.title: Understanding Git Basics
sessions.content:
Git is a distributed version‑control system that tracks changes to files over time. To start using Git, you first create a repository with `git init`, which generates a hidden `.git` folder containing all metadata. After adding files to your working directory, you must stage them with `git add <path>`; this tells Git which changes you intend to include in the next snapshot. Once staged, `git commit -m "message"` records a new commit, capturing the current state of the staged files and storing a unique SHA‑1 identifier. Commits form a directed acyclic graph, allowing you to traverse history, revert changes, or branch off. Understanding the staging area is crucial because it separates the act of editing files from the act of recording a snapshot, giving you fine‑grained control over what gets versioned. Below is a typical workflow:

```bash
# Create a new repository
mkdir my‑project && cd my‑project
git init

# Create a file and view its status
echo "Hello, Git!" > hello.txt
git status

# Stage the new file
git add hello.txt

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add hello.txt with greeting"
```

Each command interacts with the repository in a specific way: `git init` sets up the repo, `git status` shows untracked and staged files, `git add` moves changes to the index, and `git commit` records a snapshot. Mastering these basics provides the foundation for more advanced operations like branching, merging, and rebasing.

sessions.objective: Learn how to initialize a repository, stage changes, and create commits using the command line.

sessions.title: Branching and Merging
sessions.content:
Branching allows developers to work on isolated features or bug fixes without affecting the main codebase. A new branch is created with `git branch <name>`; to start working on it immediately, you can use `git checkout -b <name>`, which both creates and switches to the branch. While on a branch, you can modify files, stage, and commit as usual. When the feature is complete, you merge it back into the target branch (often `main` or `master`) using `git merge <feature-branch>`. If both branches have edited the same lines, Git will flag a merge conflict, requiring manual resolution before completing the merge. After resolving conflicts, you add the resolved files and commit the merge. Below is a typical branching workflow:

```bash
# Ensure you are on main and up to date
git checkout main
git pull

# Create and switch to a new feature branch
git checkout -b feature/login

# Make changes, stage, and commit
echo "// login logic" >> login.js
git add login.js
git commit -m "Add login feature"

# Switch back to main and merge the feature
git checkout main
git merge feature/login
```

If the merge succeeds without conflicts, Git creates a new commit that combines the histories. If conflicts arise, Git marks the conflicted files, and you must edit them to choose the desired version, then `git add` the resolved files and `git commit` to finalize the merge. Understanding these steps is essential for collaborative development and continuous integration pipelines.

sessions.objective: Learn how to create, switch, and merge branches, and understand basic conflict resolution.
